metadata.title: What Is a Flangeless Ferrule Fitting? Design, Sizes and Selection
metadata.seoTitle: What Is a Flangeless Ferrule Fitting? Design, Sizes and Selection | FOREACH
metadata.seoDescription: Learn how flangeless ferrule fittings seal rigid microfluidic tubing. Compare FOREACH HN, HN6, HNF and HNF6 dimensions, materials, port fit and installation.
metadata.coverAlt: FOREACH black, blue and natural-colored fitting nuts with separate ferrules

deck: Flangeless fittings use a threaded nut to compress a ferrule around rigid tubing, without preforming a flange. FOREACH HN, HN6, HNF and HNF6 cover tubing ODs of 1.6, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 and 3.2 mm, M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF threads, and several nut materials for reagent transfer, sample handling and wash lines in analytical instruments and laboratory automation.

leadBlocks.text: A flangeless ferrule fitting is a threaded connection for rigid microfluidic tubing. The terms flangeless fitting and ferrule fitting emphasize different features: no preformed tubing flange is needed, and a separate ferrule provides gripping and sealing. Tightening the nut compresses the ferrule around the tubing and against the receiving port. These connections can link tubing to pumps, valves and fluidic modules in reagent transfer, sample handling and wash lines.

FOREACH offers four series: HN, HN6, HNF and HNF6, with standard knurled and compact head styles. They cover tubing ODs of 1.6, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 and 3.2 mm and M6×1 or 1/4-28 UNF flat-bottom ports. For example, the illustrated HN6 has a head diameter of 6.4 mm and an overall length of 15.5 mm; check the dimensional drawing for each other series.

HN and HN6 nuts are available in PEEK, PVDF, POM and PPS; HNF uses PVDF and HNF6 uses PPS in the configurations discussed here. Separate ferrules are available in PP and ETFE. Select the nut and ferrule together for the tubing OD, fluid and installation space, and confirm the exact materials and dimensions by part number.

sections.title: What is a flangeless ferrule fitting?

blocks.text: This article covers threaded microfluidic fittings with a separate ferrule. Tubing passes through the nut and ferrule into the instrument port; tightening the nut applies axial compression. The ferrule is the sealing and gripping part around the tubing, not a hose clamp or a sanitary clamp connection.

Unlike a flanged connection, this design uses a square-cut tube end, eliminating the flange-forming step. It still requires matching tubing OD, a clean cut, the correct ferrule and a compatible receiving port.

blocks.text: The HN, HN6, HNF and HNF6 configurations discussed here use M6×1 or 1/4-28 UNF flat-bottom ports. Other geometries, threads and dedicated high-pressure fittings require their own drawings and assembly instructions.

Slide the correct nut and ferrule onto square-cut tubing in the specified orientation. Insert the assembly into the matching port while keeping the tube end in its required position. As the nut advances, it applies axial force to the ferrule, which grips the tubing and seals against the port. Sealing depends on the components seating correctly, not on thread friction alone.

blocks.alt: HN6 compact fitting, ferrule and tubing with a sectioned dimensional drawing
blocks.caption: HN6 connection example. The 6.4 mm head diameter and 15.5 mm overall length apply to the illustrated HN6, not every ferrule fitting. Follow the specified tube position and ferrule orientation.

blocks.text: If the tube end moves, the ferrule is reversed or the tubing OD is wrong, tightening resistance may increase before the sealing surfaces are seated. Additional force does not correct this mismatch and may deform the ferrule or tubing.

Check thread engagement separately from correct seating of the ferrule, tube and port. M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF are different threads; being able to start a few turns does not prove compatibility. Do not use thread tape or sealant to compensate for a mismatched sealing geometry.

sections.title: HN, HN6, HNF and HNF6: thread length and installation space

blocks.text: These FOREACH series differ in head style, material, threaded-section length, overall length and ferrule configuration. Even when thread designation and tubing OD match, compare the dimensions needed for the complete connection.

blocks.title: A 2.4 mm difference in threaded-section length: what must fit?

blocks.text: The threaded-section length is 8.1 mm for HN and HN6 and 10.5 mm for HNF and HNF6, a difference of 2.4 mm. This is the axial dimension from the head or shoulder to the front of the nut. Check it together with port depth, internal-thread position and the ferrule compression position.

blocks.text: This difference does not mean that HNF or HNF6 necessarily installs 2.4 mm deeper in the same port. Installed depth also depends on the port and ferrule seating positions. Effective thread engagement is the length over which the internal and external threads actually mate after assembly. Confirm the tube-end position separately.

The nut must compress a correctly seated ferrule while maintaining the thread engagement required by the design. If a shoulder contacts the equipment surface before the ferrule is compressed, the nut may feel fully tight while the joint still leaks. Check the dimensional fit; more torque cannot correct an axial mismatch.

The section and exploded views show the relative positions of the nut, ferrule, tubing and port. They explain the connection layout, not the dimensions or installed depth of every model in the table. Use the corresponding drawing for dimensional checks.

blocks.title: Compare head style and overall length separately

blocks.alt: FOREACH separate ferrules and fitting nuts with different head styles

blocks.text: Overall length helps assess axial space, but installed protrusion also depends on insertion depth. HN6 is 15.5 mm long versus 18.1 mm for HN. HNF6 has a compact head yet is 20.0 mm long, compared with 16.5 mm for HNF. For closely spaced ports, compare head diameter; for limited axial clearance, compare overall length, installed protrusion, tightening access and tubing routing.

blocks.text: For example, the HN and HN6 “32” nut size group covers tubing ODs of 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 and 3.2 mm. This does not mean one ferrule fits all four sizes. A 2.5 mm tube still needs a ferrule sized for 2.5 mm OD. HNF and HNF6 use individual tubing-OD configurations rather than the HN grouping rule.

blocks.title: Confirm the complete ferrule part number

blocks.text: HN and HN6 use CL-0X ferrules in OD sizes coded 16, 20, 25, 30 and 32. CL-0 and CL-0X have different geometries; the same “25” size code does not make them interchangeable. For HNF and HNF6, confirm the ferrule against the complete nut part number and approved component list before ordering or assembly.

Select nut and ferrule materials separately. PP and ETFE ferrule options must be confirmed by complete part number. A PEEK or PVDF nut does not mean all wetted surfaces in the connection have that material, and color is not a substitute for material identification.

sections.title: How does a ferrule connection differ from a flanged connection?

blocks.caption: Tube-end connection examples showing differences at the front of the fitting and in the mating components.

blocks.text: The key differences are tube-end preparation and sealing components. A flanged connection uses a preformed outward flange compressed by the nut and matching washer. A ferrule connection uses square-cut tubing and a separate ferrule to grip and seal. Select according to the existing assembly process and maintenance needs, not step count alone.

blocks.text: A flanged design may suit an established flange-forming process or prefabricated tubing assemblies. A ferrule design may suit workflows that avoid flange forming and allow ferrule replacement during maintenance. Permitted pressure, long-term sealing and reconnection limits must come from the specific assembly specifications and validation.

items.label: Flanged tubing assemblies: design and selection

blocks.text: Compression-ring connections can also avoid tube-end flanging, but their sleeves, washers and assembly method differ from the ferrule arrangement described here. “Flangeless” does not identify one universal sealing structure. See the rigid-tubing fitting guide for a comparison of the three designs.

sections.title: How to select a suitable fitting

blocks.title: Start with the port, then select tubing size and components

blocks.text: Obtain the complete port thread specification and section drawing to establish the sealing geometry. Use the actual tubing OD to select the nut and ferrule. Tubing ID and length determine internal volume, flow resistance and flow requirements. The nut through-bore is a tubing clearance dimension, not automatically the fluid-path ID.

For a 2.5 mm OD tube with HN6, select the appropriate nut size group and a CL-0X-25 ferrule, then verify the thread, nut material, ferrule material and tubing tolerances. This identifies a candidate assembly; pressure capability, chemical compatibility and installed sealing still require confirmation.

blocks.title: Match materials to the actual fluid and operating conditions

blocks.text: Specify fluid composition, concentration, operating temperature, exposure time and cleaning procedure. Check tubing, ferrule and all wetted components. Also check whether the tubing wall retains its bore and grip under assembly compression. Chemical resistance alone does not validate every wall thickness, OD tolerance or ferrule combination.

For dense port layouts, check head diameter and interference. Near enclosures, check axial clearance, tube exit direction and tool access. Provide bend allowance and movement slack so sustained pull, twist or tight bends do not load the fitting. Include new ferrules and replacement procedures in the maintenance plan.

blocks.text: Use a tubing cutter suitable for the material to obtain a square end. Remove debris and check for flattening, scratches or deformation. Confirm ferrule part number, orientation and tube-end position, then keep the assembly seated while tightening as specified. Use the method and torque confirmed for that configuration; there is no universal torque for all plastic fittings.

blocks.text: These symptoms guide troubleshooting; they do not prove a cause. For example, reduced flow may come from a different tubing ID, cutting debris or bends rather than the fitting type. Compare under controlled conditions to see whether assembly or size changes solve the problem.

blocks.title: Separate ferrule replacement from nut reuse

blocks.text: The ferrules covered here are specified for a single installation; reinstalling them may cause irreversible deformation. Prepare matching new ferrules for maintenance. Inspect the gripped tube end and rework it if required. Assess nut reuse separately by inspecting its threads and load-bearing surfaces; replacing the sealing component does not automatically mean replacing the whole fitting.

blocks.title: Validate the complete connection in the fluidic system

blocks.text: Check leaks, tube movement and flow under defined fluid, temperature and pressure conditions; check air ingress on suction lines. Then cover actual start/stop cycles, pulsation, temperature changes and motion, recording test duration, cycles and allowable leakage. A static pressure-hold pass applies only to those test conditions, not full instrument operation.

Permitted pressure depends on the complete nut, ferrule, tubing and port combination. Do not transfer a dedicated high-pressure fitting rating to HN, HN6, HNF or HNF6. A stronger nut material alone does not increase the allowable pressure of the entire fluid path.

faqItems.question: Are flangeless fittings always tool-free?
faqItems.answer: No. Hand tightening, a dedicated driver and torque-controlled tools are configuration-specific. Flangeless means that no tube-end flange is preformed; it does not guarantee that every model can be installed by feel alone.

faqItems.question: Are CL-0 and CL-0X interchangeable at the same tubing OD?
faqItems.answer: Not on OD alone. Their geometries differ and must match the nut and port. Confirm complete part numbers and the approved component combination; trial tightening or extra force does not establish compatibility.

faqItems.question: Do compact fittings withstand more pressure than standard knurled fittings?
faqItems.answer: Head style does not determine pressure capability. Compact heads concern installation space; permitted pressure also depends on ferrule, tubing, port, temperature and assembly conditions. Check and validate the specific combination.

faqItems.question: Does tubing ID matter when both tubes have 1.6 mm OD?
faqItems.answer: Yes. OD matches the nut and ferrule, while ID affects flow resistance, internal volume and wall thickness. Confirm how the tube wall behaves under compression as well as the actual flow, pressure and fluid requirements.
